title: Manage What Matters
hook: Green dashboard: revenue up, NPS steady. Three of four strategic choices reversed by daily decisions. No metric for that.
counterintuition: A management system that everyone follows exactly can still kill a strategy. When the reviews, measures, and rewards were built for the previous strategic choices, every team member doing their job correctly is compounding the problem.
tryThisNow: After your next review meeting, list the three things that were measured or reported. Ask: if the strategy were actually working, which of those numbers would look different? If none would change, the system is reporting on the past, not reinforcing the strategy. Name one decision the review should have forced and did not.
keyTakeaway: The management system is the fifth strategic choice: the reviews, measures, and rewards that must reinforce the first four, or they will quietly undo them.

breakdown.fastRead:
Simon's retail chain had changed its strategy eighteen months ago: from new customer acquisition to loyalty and repeat purchase depth. The choices were approved by the board. The commission structure was not updated. The team was still paid for new accounts.

Every quarterly review showed green: acquisition targets hit, new accounts up, team morale positive. The loyalty metrics were not on any review slide.

Eighteen months after the strategy changed, the top three performers by commission were the three reps who had done the least work on repeat customer engagement.

A strategy is not complete when the choices are made. It is complete when the management systems reward the behavior the choices require.
breakdown.deepRead:
The fifth strategic choice is the management system: the reviews, measures, and accountability routines that reinforce the first four choices or quietly undermine them. A management system becomes a problem not by failing but by succeeding at the wrong thing. If the reviews measure the previous strategy's priorities and the compensation rewards the previous strategy's behaviors, the system performs exactly as designed: driving effort toward the old direction while the new strategy is officially in place.

The distinction between a genuine strategy review and corporate theater is whether the review could actually change a decision. A review that cannot change a decision is not a strategy review. It is a briefing.

The difference shows up in the questions being asked. A genuine strategy review asks: is this working and why? It invites new information that might reverse a decision. Corporate theater asks: are we on track to the plan we already committed to? That question defends a position and validates work already done. The review may surface a problem. But the format has no mechanism for using that problem to change what the organization does next.

A review built for the previous strategy performs corporate theater regardless of the new strategic language used to describe it. The measures were designed to report on different choices. The accountability routines ask questions the previous strategy needed answered. The decisions most in need of revisiting are the ones the review format cannot raise.
breakdown.fullRead:
Management systems are the most common way a strategy is killed without anyone deciding to kill it. The strategic choices are made. The leadership team approves them. Execution begins. And then the reviews continue to measure the previous strategy's metrics, the compensation continues to reward the previous strategy's behavior, and the accountability routines continue to ask the questions the previous strategy needed answered.

No one decides to undermine the new strategy. The system does it automatically, because the system was never updated to point in the new direction.

The test for any management system is one question: if the strategy were actually working, which of these numbers would look different? If the answer is none of the numbers the system currently tracks, the system is not reinforcing the strategy. It is a legacy measurement running undisturbed while the strategy tries to move in a different direction.

A sales organization that shifts from new account acquisition to renewal and expansion revenue but keeps its commission structure weighted toward new accounts will have a clear outcome: the team will optimize for new accounts. The measure drives the behavior. If the behavior the measure drives is not the behavior the strategy requires, the system is working perfectly in the wrong direction.

Think about the last review meeting you participated in. What were the three main things reported? Were they things that would look different if the new strategy were working, or things that measured adherence to a plan already committed to? If the answer is adherence, the review was not checking whether the strategy is working. It was confirming that everyone did what they agreed to do. Those are different conversations. Only the first one can change what happens next.

The second test is whether the review could have reversed a decision. If every agenda item was a confirmation of a committed plan, the meeting was a briefing. If at least one agenda item allowed the group to look at evidence and ask whether the strategic choice is working, the meeting was a strategy review. The difference is not the frequency or the attendees. It is whether new information could change a decision that was previously made.

Reviews that cannot change decisions are not neutral. They actively reinforce whatever direction the current metrics point. If those metrics were designed for the previous strategy, the review is reinforcing the previous strategy every time it runs, at every level of the organization, without anyone intending it to.

Name one review that your team runs regularly. Ask what decision it could change if the information were worse than expected. If the answer is nothing changes, the review is corporate theater. That is not a judgment; it is a design problem. The management system can be redesigned to ask the question the strategy requires.

examples.title: Rachel Sees Six Months of Green Velocity and Declining Retention

planSpec.domain: a software product team redesigning its weekly sprint review after the strategy shifted from feature velocity to retention depth
planSpec.audience: a product manager whose team still reports ticket throughput in every review even though the strategic choice shifted to engagement quality
planSpec.stakes: the review format creates invisible pressure to keep building features while the retention metric declines unreported
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rachel reviews six months of sprint reports and finds the misalignment between the review metric and the new strategic choice is the source of the stall

examples.scenario: Rachel reviewed six months of sprint decks. Every single one celebrated a green velocity number in the top right corner. Every single one was missing the retention chart. She went back to the retention data separately and found that the rate had declined in four of the six months covered by those green reviews. The team had been accountable for throughput and hitting targets on throughput. No one had been accountable for retention depth because retention depth was not on any review slide. The system had reinforced exactly the wrong behavior: building faster toward the old strategic priority while the new one slowly worsened.
examples.whatToDo: Replace velocity as the primary sprint review metric with the retention depth measure the new strategy requires. Remove throughput reporting from the standard review agenda or move it to an appendix. The change signals to the team which behavior the review now holds them accountable for.
examples.whyItMatters: A review format that measures the previous strategy's priorities rewards the previous strategy's behavior regardless of what strategic choices were made six months ago. The sprint review is not a neutral report; it is the system that tells the team what they are accountable for.

examples.title: Luke Asks Which Number Would Change If the New Strategy Were Working

planSpec.domain: a hospital department restructuring its monthly leadership review after shifting strategic emphasis to preventive care
planSpec.audience: a department chief whose monthly review was designed for the acute treatment volume strategy
planSpec.stakes: the review measures the old strategy's outputs while the preventive care initiative has no visibility and no accountability
planSpec.requiredBeat: Luke asks which of the three reported numbers would change if the preventive care initiative were working, and no one answers

examples.scenario: At 2:00 p.m., Luke walks into the monthly leadership review and sees the standard agenda printed on the table: bed occupancy, procedure counts, average length of stay. Three numbers. All three were designed to measure acute treatment volume. He sits down and asks the group a question before the first slide: which of those three numbers would look different next month if our preventive care initiative were working? Silence. Then someone says: none of them. The systems are reporting on the old strategy. The new one is invisible, unmeasured, and unaccountable.
examples.whatToDo: Before the next monthly review, name the one or two measures that would show the preventive care initiative is gaining traction: early-intervention referral counts, screening completion rates, patient re-enrollment in wellness programs. Replace one of the existing agenda items with one of those measures to make the new strategy visible in the review.
examples.whyItMatters: A review that cannot show whether the new strategy is working is not a strategy review. It is a performance report for the previous strategy. The gap becomes visible when the question is asked: which of these numbers would look different if the new strategy were working?

examples.title: Niklas Hears What the Commission Structure Is Actually Saying

planSpec.domain: a sales organization redesigning compensation after shifting from volume-based to customer-success-based strategy
planSpec.audience: a sales director whose team is compensated on new deals closed but whose strategy now emphasizes expansion revenue and renewal rates
planSpec.stakes: the commission structure is actively pushing the best people away from the new strategy and toward the behavior the old strategy rewarded
planSpec.requiredBeat: Niklas's top rep tells him the commission structure is rewarding exactly the opposite of what the strategy now requires and she is about to leave

examples.scenario: 'I spend seventy percent of my time on renewal calls. I get paid for zero percent of it.' Niklas's top rep said it quietly after the team meeting, not in front of the room. She was not complaining about the work. She was pointing at the management system. The commission report from last quarter showed her at the bottom: the lowest new-deal commission of anyone on the team. The renewal-rate leaderboard showed her at the top. The new strategy said renewal and expansion were the priority. The commission structure said new accounts were. She was about to start job-searching because the system was telling her the new strategy was not the real one.
examples.whatToDo: Redesign the commission structure so renewal and expansion revenue carries equal or greater weight than new account acquisition. The change does not require announcing a new culture; it requires changing the number that appears on the rep's commission statement. That is the communication that changes behavior.
examples.whyItMatters: A commission structure is not a neutral financial instrument. It is the management system's most direct communication about which behavior the strategy actually values. When the commission and the stated strategy point in different directions, the commission wins.

examples.title: Paula Rebuilds the Client Review to Show What the New Position Requires

planSpec.domain: a creative agency restructuring its client success review after pivoting from output quantity to campaign effectiveness
planSpec.audience: a managing director whose client reviews measure deliverable completion rates and budget adherence
planSpec.stakes: the review measures the old strategic position's outputs while the new position requires effectiveness evidence the current system cannot show
planSpec.requiredBeat: before: client asks a third time if the campaign moved behavior; after: Paula rebuilds the review around two effectiveness measures the new position requires

examples.scenario: The conference room smells of cold coffee and printed slide decks: nine slides of deliverable checkboxes and one slide that says campaign results: data collection ongoing. Before: Paula runs the client review showing on-time delivery rates and budget variance. Both are green. The client asks for the third time whether the campaign moved any customer behavior. The review format has no answer for that question. It was designed for an agency that sold outputs. The new positioning sells effectiveness. After: Paula rebuilds the review template around two leading effectiveness indicators she can report monthly: behavioral signal rate from the campaign's target cohort and assisted conversion attribution. The client stops asking the question because the review now answers it.
examples.whatToDo: Identify the one or two leading indicators of effectiveness that the new strategic position requires the agency to report. Replace the delivery compliance slides with those indicators in the standard client review template. The new format is the management system that makes the new position visible and accountable.
examples.whyItMatters: A client review built around delivery compliance reinforces a delivery-focused strategic position even when the agency has formally committed to an effectiveness-focused one. The review format is not cosmetic; it is the system that determines what the agency is accountable for in every client relationship.

examples.title: Janek's Promotion Data Shows Three Years of the Wrong Strategy

planSpec.domain: a university department restructuring its annual faculty review after shifting emphasis from research publications to industry partnership outcomes
planSpec.audience: a department head whose annual review process was designed for the research-ranking strategy
planSpec.stakes: the promotion system assigns zero weight to industry partnership outcomes, systematically promoting the old strategy while leadership formally commits to the new one
planSpec.requiredBeat: three years of promotion decisions reveal a systematic pattern that shows the misalignment between the management system and the strategic choice

examples.scenario: Janek reviewed three years of promotion committee notes. Every faculty member promoted to associate professor had a strong publications record and weak industry involvement. Two faculty members with strong industry partnership records and moderate publication counts had been denied in the same period. The committee had made reasonable decisions given the criteria the system used. But the criteria were the criteria of the research-ranking strategy the department had formally changed two years ago. The promotion system had made the decision every year that the management system required: reward publications. The new strategy was on the letterhead. It was not in the rubric.
examples.whatToDo: Before the next promotion cycle, revise the review rubric to include industry partnership outcomes at a weight that reflects the new strategic emphasis. The change must be in the rubric, not in the committee's instructions. Instructions are interpreted; rubrics are applied.
examples.whyItMatters: A promotion system that measures citation counts and journal tier for a department that has committed to an industry partnership strategy will systematically produce promotion decisions that reward the old strategy. The pattern shows up across multiple cycles, not as individual errors but as a management system performing exactly as designed.

examples.title: Camille Imagines the Combined P&L Conversation and Sees the Problem

planSpec.domain: a family business restructuring its monthly review after adding a second product line with a different margin and growth profile
planSpec.audience: an operations director whose review format cannot distinguish performance drivers for the two lines
planSpec.stakes: the combined reporting makes the new line's low margins trigger cost-cutting conversations that suppress the growth investment it requires
planSpec.requiredBeat: Camille imagines presenting the combined P&L to her father and sees that the reporting structure makes the new line look like a problem every month

examples.scenario: You imagine standing at the whiteboard in front of Camille's father, the founder, presenting the combined month-end P&L. The new product line has low margins and fast growth. The mature line has high margins and slow growth. Combined, they produce a number that looks mediocre. Camille has run this mental exercise three times. Each time she gets to the margin line, she can predict the conversation: the new line's losses will trigger a cost-cutting discussion that will pull investment from exactly the initiative that needs it most. The management system does not distinguish two different strategies. It treats both product lines as one. Every month the combined P&L sends the same signal: the margins are lower than they should be. Every month the new line loses the investment argument.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the two product lines in the monthly review structure and use different performance measures for each based on their respective strategic positions. Present the mature line on margin and cash contribution. Present the new line on revenue growth rate and market signal indicators. The review must distinguish two strategies to reinforce both.
examples.whyItMatters: A combined P&L that aggregates two lines with different strategic profiles makes the new line look like a problem every time its low margins are averaged against the mature line's high ones. The review structure is suppressing investment in the growth strategy by measuring it against the wrong standard.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a genuine strategy review from corporate theater?
choices: A genuine strategy review could actually change a decision based on new information; corporate theater validates adherence to an already-committed plan and cannot generate new decisions.
A genuine strategy review focuses on long-term metrics; corporate theater focuses on short-term quarterly performance.
A genuine strategy review is led by the CEO; corporate theater is delegated to middle management reporting.
questions.explanation: The defining characteristic is whether new information in the review can change what the organization decides to do. A review designed to validate adherence to a plan asks whether we are on track, not whether the track is right. That question defends a committed position and cannot generate new decisions, which is the definition of corporate theater.

questions.prompt: A sales organization shifted strategy from new account acquisition to renewal and expansion revenue six months ago. The commission structure still pays primarily for new accounts. Which action is the necessary management system alignment?
choices: Brief the team on the new strategy at the next all-hands and reinforce the importance of renewal focus.
Redesign the commission structure so that renewal and expansion revenue carries equal or greater weight than new account acquisition, aligning the reward with the new strategic choice.
Add renewal rates to the monthly performance dashboard alongside new account metrics and report both.
questions.explanation: Briefing the team changes awareness, not incentive. Adding renewals to the dashboard without changing the commission leaves the existing reward in place. The management system must change the compensation, not just the reporting, to make the new strategic behavior the one that gets rewarded.

questions.prompt: A product team shifted strategy from feature velocity to retention depth six months ago. Sprint reviews still report ticket throughput and velocity scores. Retention has never appeared on a review slide. Which action most aligns the management system with the strategy?
choices: Continue the current sprint review format but add a verbal retention update at the end of each meeting.
Replace the sprint review with a monthly strategic review covering all product metrics at once.
Replace velocity as the primary sprint review metric with the retention depth measure the new strategy requires, and remove throughput reporting from the standard agenda.
questions.explanation: A verbal update leaves velocity as the primary metric, which still signals what the team is accountable for. A monthly strategic review does not change the sprint review that is reinforcing the old strategy every two weeks. Replacing the primary metric removes the old reward signal and puts the new strategy's required measure at the center of the review.

questions.prompt: A hospital department shifted strategic emphasis from acute treatment volume to preventive care. The monthly leadership review still covers bed occupancy, procedure counts, and average length of stay. The preventive care initiative has no visibility in the review. What is the primary reason the new strategy is not gaining traction?
choices: The review measures what mattered under the old strategy, making the leadership team accountable for the old strategy's outputs while the new one remains invisible and unreinforced in the management system.
The leadership team lacks commitment to the preventive care initiative and needs stronger direction from the chief medical officer.
The preventive care initiative needs more time to generate measurable outcomes before it can be incorporated into the leadership review.
questions.explanation: Commitment and timeline are not the primary diagnosis. The review measures the old strategy's priorities and holds leaders accountable for the old strategy's outputs. The new strategy has no measure in the review, which means it has no reinforcement mechanism. The management system is actively rewarding the old direction, not failing to reward the new one.

questions.prompt: A creative agency shifted from output quantity to campaign effectiveness. The client review template measures deliverable completion and budget adherence. A client has asked three times whether the campaign moved customer behavior. Which management system change is most needed?
choices: Add a slide at the end of the client review showing effectiveness metrics collected so far.
Replace deliverable completion and budget adherence with effectiveness measures the agency can report monthly, making the review accountable to the new strategic position.
Schedule a separate effectiveness review alongside the existing delivery review to address the client's recurring question.
questions.explanation: A slide at the end or a parallel review both leave the primary template in place, continuing to reward delivery compliance. The management system change must make effectiveness the primary measure in the client review and remove the delivery measures that reinforce the old strategic position. Adding alongside is not alignment; it is addition.

questions.prompt: A university department formally committed to industry partnership outcomes two years ago. Three years of promotion data show that every faculty member promoted to associate professor had strong publication records and weak industry involvement. Two faculty with strong partnerships were denied. What does this pattern reveal?
choices: The promotion system weighted publications and ignored partnership outcomes: three years of decisions rewarding the old research-first strategy while leadership formally committed to a different one.
The promotion committee made reasonable decisions given the evidence available at each review cycle.
The department needs to clarify the new strategic emphasis to the promotion committee before the next cycle.
questions.explanation: The committee decisions were correct given the criteria the system used. The problem is the criteria themselves: promotion processes built for the old strategy reward the old behavior regardless of what leadership formally commits to. Three years of data show a systematic management system problem, not a series of individual committee errors.

questions.prompt: A family business presents both a mature product line and a new product line as a combined P&L. The mature line has high margins; the new line has low margins and fast growth. Every month the combined number triggers a cost-cutting conversation that suppresses investment in the new line. Which management system change is most needed?
choices: Adjust the new product line's margin targets to be closer to the mature line's historical margins.
Continue combined reporting for one more year before evaluating whether separation is warranted.
Separate the two product lines in the review, apply metrics suited to each line's strategic profile, and present them independently so each is evaluated on its own terms.
questions.explanation: Adjusting margin targets holds the new line to the wrong standard. Waiting extends the period in which combined reporting suppresses investment in the growth line. The management system must separate the lines so the different strategies governing each can be measured and rewarded independently, without one line's performance penalizing the other.

questions.prompt: A sales director's top-performing rep by commission has the lowest renewal-rate contribution. The rep with the highest renewal rate has the lowest commission check of the quarter. What does this pattern indicate about the management system?
choices: The top-performing rep has a more effective approach and the organization should recognize and replicate that pattern.

The commission structure is actively rewarding the behavior the new strategy wants to eliminate and penalizing the behavior the new strategy requires, making the management system work directly against the strategic choice.
The renewal-focused rep needs additional coaching to improve new account performance alongside renewal work.
questions.explanation: The commission-to-renewal inversion reveals that the management system rewards the old strategic behavior and penalizes the new one. This is not a rep capability problem; it is a design problem. The system is performing exactly as designed: rewarding new account acquisition, which is the opposite of what the new strategy requires.

questions.prompt: A hospital department chief has two options: Option A, add early-intervention referral counts and screening rates to the monthly review alongside existing acute care metrics; Option B, remove bed occupancy and procedure counts from the monthly review and redesign the agenda around preventive care measures. Which is the stronger management system response?
choices: Option A, because it shows the leadership team is taking the new strategy seriously without disrupting the accountability structure that already works.
Both equally, because each addresses the management system gap in a way appropriate to different organizational contexts.

Option B, because Option A adds preventive care measures without removing the acute care metrics that still drive the primary accountability signal; the old strategy's rewards remain fully intact and the review continues to primarily reinforce the previous direction.
questions.explanation: Option A adds new measurement without removing the old measure. The existing metrics still dominate the review's accountability logic, meaning the old strategy's rewards remain active. Option B redesigns the review to reinforce the new strategy and removes the mechanism that continues to reward the old one. Management system alignment requires replacing the old rewards, not adding new ones alongside them.

reviewCards.front: What distinguishes a strategy review from corporate theater?
reviewCards.back: A strategy review is one that could actually change a decision based on new information. Corporate theater validates adherence to a plan already committed to. The difference shows up in the question being asked: is this working and why, or are we on track to what we already agreed?

reviewCards.front: What is the management system test for strategy alignment?
reviewCards.back: Ask: if the strategy were actually working, which of the numbers the system currently tracks would look different? If none would change, the system is measuring the previous strategy's priorities, not reinforcing the new one.

reviewCards.front: What happens when a commission structure is not updated after a strategic shift?
reviewCards.back: The commission continues to reward the old strategy's behavior. The team optimizes for what the commission pays for. The new strategy's priorities are reported but not rewarded, which means they are not fully pursued regardless of what the leadership team communicates.

reviewCards.front: Name three management system elements that most often undermine a new strategy passively.
reviewCards.back: Reviews measure what the previous strategy needed tracked. Compensation rewards what the previous strategy valued. Accountability routines ask questions the previous strategy needed answered. The system rewards the old direction automatically, with no one deciding to undermine the new one.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean when a review could not force any decision?
reviewCards.back: It means the review was a briefing, not a strategy review. A review that cannot change what the organization decides to do next is a performance report for the previous strategy, not a management system aligned to the new one.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to audit management systems by asking which behavior each review, measure, and accountability routine currently rewards and whether that behavior is the behavior the strategy requires. You practice the alignment test: if the strategy were actually working, which numbers would look different?

ifThenPlans.context: after a strategic choice is made or approved
ifThenPlans.plan: Before ending the planning session, name the one review, measure, or accountability routine that most needs to change for the new strategy to be reinforced. Schedule that change in the same planning cycle, not as a later implementation task.

ifThenPlans.context: when a team is consistently not executing a new strategic direction
ifThenPlans.plan: Check whether the compensation, review structure, or accountability system is still rewarding the old behavior. Consistent non-execution is more often a management system problem than a commitment problem.

ifThenPlans.context: when designing a new performance review format
ifThenPlans.plan: Start with the strategic choices, not with the available metrics. Ask which specific behaviors the strategy requires and design the review to make those behaviors visible and accountable. Remove metrics that reinforce different strategic priorities.

ifThenPlans.context: when a review shows green across all metrics but strategic progress is unclear
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask which green metric would look different if the new strategy were actually working. If none would change, the review is measuring the wrong things and the strategy is invisible to the management system.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: After your next team review, write down the three things the review measured or reported. For each one, ask: would this number look different if the strategy were working? If none would change, name one specific measure that would show strategic progress and one specific review question that could not be answered today.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, after a review meeting or performance check-in, ask whether the questions being asked could have changed a decision. If the questions were all about adherence to an already-committed plan, the review was corporate theater. Name one question the review should have asked but did not.

memorableLines.text: A strategy is not complete when the choices are made. It is complete when the management systems reward the behavior the choices require.
memorableLines.why: The two-sentence definition places the management system inside the strategy itself, not as an implementation step that follows strategy.

memorableLines.text: A review that cannot change a decision is not a strategy review. It is a briefing.
memorableLines.why: The two-sentence contrast gives the reader a portable test they can apply to any review they run or attend.

memorableLines.text: The test for any management system is one question: if the strategy were actually working, which of these numbers would look different?
memorableLines.why: The single-question test compresses the alignment audit into a form the reader can apply immediately to any dashboard, review template, or commission structure.
